#348. Octopus Energy releases plug-in solar kit for small businesses

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (299 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Octopus Energy releases plug-in solar kit for small businesses

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (299 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UK-based Octopus Energy has expanded its plug-in solar offering to small businesses, targeting cafés, shops, hairdressers and offices, particularly those operating from rented premises or buildings unsuitable for conventional rooftop PV installations.
  • Recent findings suggest that the kits feature 460 W bifacial solar panels that can be mounted on walls or placed on the ground and connected directly to a weatherproof outdoor socket without professional installation.
  • In a recent development, according to Octopus Energy, a small business installing two panels could reduce its annual electricity bill by up to 23%, depending on consumption, solar generation and export revenues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UK-based Octopus Energy has expanded its plug-in solar offering to small businesses, targeting cafés, shops, hairdressers and offices, particularly those operating from rented premises or buildings unsuitable for conventional rooftop PV installations.

Recent findings suggest that the kits feature 460 W bifacial solar panels that can be mounted on walls or placed on the ground and connected directly to a weatherproof outdoor socket without professional installation. The portable systems are available in one- or two-panel configurations, with prices starting at GBP 450 ($594).

In a recent development, according to Octopus Energy, a small business installing two panels could reduce its annual electricity bill by up to 23%, depending on consumption, solar generation and export revenues. The tech giant estimates that a two-panel system costing GBP 650 could achieve payback in as little as three years when combined with self-consumption and a suitable electricity export tariff.

In a recent development, the business launch follows the introduction of plug-in solar kits for UK households in August 2026, after regulatory changes enabled their use. Octopus said the initial residential offering sold out within two weeks.

The move is part of the manufacturer’s broader strategy to make distributed energy technologies more accessible to households and smaller electricity consumers.

In July, Octopus unveiled its Nook residential battery range, including the 2 kWh Nook Cube, which connects to a standard household socket and can be expanded to 10.5 kWh, and the 5 kWh wall-mounted Nook Colossus, expandable to 30 kWh. The storage systems are scheduled to launch in the UK in 2027, followed by Germany, France, Italy and Spain.

Octopus cited a YouGov survey of 1,034 UK small and medium-sized business decision-makers showing that 62% recognize the potential of solar power to reduce electricity costs, while only 18% have installed it.

#347. Industry News: PVcase releases early-stage feasibility and design software

Industry News: PVcase releases early-stage feasibility and design software

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Solar development platform provider PVCase has introduced PVcase Concept, a latest cloud-based software tool for early-stage site feasibility and design.
  • According to the tech giant, the fresh software addresses “the missing middle” of the solar development process, sitting between the site selection process and more detailed engineering of a project that is already finalized, and also serves as a filter to give utility-scale development teams an organized way to arrive at a “go or no-go” decision about a project.
  • “Every site in a pipeline starts as a ‘maybe,’ and too many stay that way too long, pulling engineering time into projects that won’t get built,” noted PVcase CEO David Trainavicius in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solar development platform provider PVCase has introduced PVcase Concept, a latest cloud-based software tool for early-stage site feasibility and design.

According to the tech giant, the fresh software addresses “the missing middle” of the solar development process, sitting between the site selection process and more detailed engineering of a project that is already finalized, and also serves as a filter to give utility-scale development teams an organized way to arrive at a “go or no-go” decision about a project.

“Every site in a pipeline starts as a ‘maybe,’ and too many stay that way too long, pulling engineering time into projects that won’t get built,” noted PVcase CEO David Trainavicius in a statement. “PVcase Concept closes the gap between finding a site and engineering it, with a single source of truth for the go/no-go decision. The right sites move from maybe to megawatts faster, and fewer engineering hours are lost on the rest.”.

The software helps development teams after the site screening process by bringing in site data from PVcase Prospect software or importing their own KML, KMZ, or shapefiles, and then using the software to conduct buildable area analysis based on GIS data, produce a preliminary design and compare layout options based on financial metrics like CapEx and LCOE.

If the decision is made to move forward on a project, the preliminary design and underlying data can be moved into PVcase Ground Mount to allow a developer’s engineering team to complete a final design.

In an interview with pv magazine USA, PVcase senior VP of engineering Karen Djoury explained that project attrition is becoming a major concern for developers, with 46% of respondents to the organization’s recent survey on the state of project development indicating that at least half their projects never reach construction.

Recent findings suggest that djoury mentioned that in many cases, developers have access to the information that would help developers reject a site before dedicating too many resources, but that data is not well-organized. “It’s not that there’s a lack of data but it’s a lack of control of data,” she explained. “The go/no-go decision can become hard if you can’t keep track of your assumptions all the time.”.

Djoury’s words are a call-back to the “single source of truth” Trainavicius discussed. The PVcase Concept software is designed to collect information about policy rules, geography, prospective equipment, costs and production estimates in a single dashboard that can give development teams a clear idea of whether a project will face major obstacles to completion.

PVcase product manager JP Baertson presented a demo of the newly introduced Concept software to pv magazine USA, in which he showed how the software displayed data about an example project in western Michigan.

Given a group of polygons overlaid on an aerial map, the software identified buildable and non-buildable areas as defined by underlying GIS data from PVcase’s Prospect database, adding setbacks based on site features and local regulations and identifying local transmission lines and points of interconnection.

Another location-based feature of the software highlights government regulations like Clean Water Act restrictions that apply to the site, and also provides an AI-generated indication of local community sentiment, gleaned from news postings and public meeting minutes.

Baertson pointed out that policy considerations have become more important to developers, citing an example of a PVcase customer whose utility-scale project pipeline has tripled in recent years. “Guess what else has tripled?” he asked. “The amount of attrition. They’re still seeing the same amount actually get to construction-ready. And so that level of go/no-go decision is almost always tripping them up at the policy level, not necessarily the design or cost-of-materials level. And that’s the type of thing we want to make sure we’re surfacing as early as possible.”.

The software allows developers to use the automatically generated information or add manual overrides to the buildable areas, for example, in places where landowners are interested in removing a stand or trees, or where the software identifies a slope that could be graded without a great deal of cost.

At that point, the software can automatically fill the buildable areas of the site with a proposed system layout with module rows, inverters and other equipment, based on a specified Ground Coverage Ratio (GCR). The software is pre-populated with a component database consisting of thousands of entries that allows developers to choose the equipment they wish to spec out for the site — and change that equipment and GCR on the fly to see how it affects the outcomes.

In PVcase Concept, those outcomes are measured in system size and total expected annual energy yield. The system can also generate expected costs for capital and operating expenses, ultimately providing an estimated number for levelized cost of energy (LCOE). All of that is also subject to manual adjustment based on the developer’s specific costs and what-if analysis.

Each mix of preliminary design and estimated financial performance in the software can be saved as a scenario, and these scenarios are what provides the software’s users with the ability to make an ultimate decision about a project.

“This is a way for [developers] to look at multiple iterations of this for the team to make financial calls, go/no-go decisions across the actual landowners,” Baertson explained. “And then the reality of ‘Can we move this forward? Let’s figure that out now before we’ve paid our consultant, before we’ve paid our engineering team to do this, and bring in some of those decisions at this stage that really bring reality to us sooner versus bad news down the line after more than a couple thousand dollars have been spent.’”.

If the team chooses to move forward with the project, the Concept software allows a scenario to be output as a DXF file, which Baertson described as “turnkey perfect for a PVcase Ground Mount CAD tool,” or any other CAD tool.

The PVcase Concept software is available worldwide as a standalone solution or integrated with PVcase Prospect in the United States starting on Nov. 16, 2026. PVcase executives and engineers will be on hand at RE+ 2026 to discuss the software.

AI model detects small fires, smoke in PV plants

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A research team from Chinese state-owned utility China Huaneng Group has developed a latest deep-learning framework for real-time fire and smoke detection in PV power plants.
  • Dubbed PVFire-YOLO, the system is designed to detect small flames and smoke plumes while reducing false alarms caused by sunlight reflected from PV module surfaces.
  • “For the specific domain of PV inspection, deep-learning research has concentrated on three problems: electroluminescence (EL) crack detection, infrared (IR) hot-spot localization, and panel-level visible-light anomaly detection such as surface defects and soiling,” the researchers remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A research team from Chinese state-owned utility China Huaneng Group has developed a latest deep-learning framework for real-time fire and smoke detection in PV power plants.

Dubbed PVFire-YOLO, the system is designed to detect small flames and smoke plumes while reducing false alarms caused by sunlight reflected from PV module surfaces.

“For the specific domain of PV inspection, deep-learning research has concentrated on three problems: electroluminescence (EL) crack detection, infrared (IR) hot-spot localization, and panel-level visible-light anomaly detection such as surface defects and soiling,” the researchers remarked. “Fire detection in PV environments has, by contrast, received almost no dedicated treatment.”.

The researchers noted they compiled the first annotated flame-and-smoke dataset specifically designed for PV environments.

“The new annotated corpus, PV-Fire, combines surveillance and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery from operating utility-scale plants with controlled outdoor burns staged among real PV modules,” they added.

The proposed method is based on the YOLOv12 real-time object detection model and incorporates three additional components to improve fire detection in PV environments. A patch-aware attention block enhances weak flame and smoke features, while a gather-and-distribute mechanism combines information across four feature levels. An adaptive fusion head adds a high-resolution detection branch to identify small targets.

According to recent reports, the researchers assembled the PV-Fire dataset, comprising 5,824 images with 9,107 annotated flame and smoke objects. The dataset combines surveillance and drone imagery, controlled outdoor burns, and synthetic images. They allocated 4,070 images for training, 870 for validation, and 884 for testing. They also separated scenes across the three subsets and restricted synthetic images to the training set.

Industry observers note that the team compared PVFire-YOLO with 14 existing detection models using the PV-Fire dataset, including Faster R-CNN, transformer-based models, and several YOLO variants. They also benchmarked it against 13 alternative models using the publicly available D-Fire dataset.

According to recent reports, the tests assessed detection accuracy, small-target performance, false alarms caused by reflections, cross-dataset generalization, and processing speed on desktop and embedded hardware. The results were averaged across three training runs.

PVFire-YOLO achieved a mean average precision of 87.4% at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.5 (mAP@50) on the PV-Fire dataset. The figure was 85.0% when testing was restricted to footage from operating PV plants and 84.4% on the D-Fire dataset.

Compared with the baseline YOLOv12 model, the proposed method improved small-target average precision by 5.2 percentage points. It also reduced the reflection-related false-positive rate to 3.1% while detecting a higher proportion of actual flame and smoke targets.

“Running at 79 frames/s on an RTX 3090 desktop graphics card and 21 frames/s on a Jetson Orin Nano compact AI computer, the model meets the latency budget for real-time edge deployment in distributed plant monitoring,” the researchers concluded. “Future work will extend the corpus to plants in diverse climates, incorporate temporal filtering to suppress isolated false positives, and fuse visible light detection with infrared thermal imaging to enhance robustness under adverse illumination.”.

The findings are presented in the study “Real time small target fire detection in photovoltaic plants using attention enhanced multiscale fusion,” published in Scientific Reports.

#345. Breaking: HoloSolis raises €15 million, welcomes four fresh shareholders

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (368 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Breaking: HoloSolis raises €15 million, welcomes four fresh shareholders

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (368 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • French PV manufacturer HoloSolis has completed a Series A funding round of more than €15 million ($16.5 million), bringing in four new shareholders: French banking group Crédit Agricole, through four of its regional banks; investment management firm Algebris; Chinese solar module manufacturer Trina Solar; and Chinese EV charging and energy storage specialist StarCharge.
  • The new investors join existing shareholders, including European cleantech investor EIT InnoEnergy, French industrial property developer IDEC Group, independent power producer TSE, and investment holding company Calès Technologies.
  • Sources indicate that trina Solar is already a strategic technology partner in the project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French PV manufacturer HoloSolis has completed a Series A funding round of more than €15 million ($16.5 million), bringing in four new shareholders: French banking group Crédit Agricole, through four of its regional banks; investment management firm Algebris; Chinese solar module manufacturer Trina Solar; and Chinese EV charging and energy storage specialist StarCharge.

The new investors join existing shareholders, including European cleantech investor EIT InnoEnergy, French industrial property developer IDEC Group, independent power producer TSE, and investment holding company Calès Technologies.

Sources indicate that trina Solar is already a strategic technology partner in the project. In September 2025, HoloSolis signed a licensing agreement covering Trina Solar’s tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) patents for European manufacturing. The two companies subsequently signed a strategic cooperation agreement in December 2025 to support development of the French factory.

In a recent development, the latest funding will enable HoloSolis to continue preparatory work for its planned manufacturing facility in Hambach, in France’s Moselle department. The factory is designed to reach an annual production capacity of 5 GW of solar cells and modules, equivalent to approximately 10 million panels.

Industry observers note that the €850 million project is expected to create approximately 1,900 direct jobs. HoloSolis stated it has secured letters of intent from prospective customers covering more than 30 GW of future production.

The manufacturer looks to use the latest financing to finalize detailed engineering studies, prepare technical specifications, select equipment suppliers for its production lines, and qualify solar module prototypes.

In a recent development, holoSolis filed a construction permit application for the Hambach site in April 2024. The project subsequently received French government recognition as a project of national interest. HoloSolis has also secured more than €220 million in initial financing, including support under France’s green industry investment tax credit scheme.

The manufacturer aims to begin production in 2027 and gradually ramp up to its full annual capacity of 5 GW by 2030.

Sources indicate that the latest fundraising also follows HoloSolis’ selection for financial support under the European Union’s Innovation Fund in October 2026. The project was among 12 cleantech manufacturing initiatives selected in a funding round covering solar manufacturing, batteries, heat pumps, electrolyzers and other technologies.

It has been revealed that architecture in Brazil this month brings questions of cultural identity, environmental resilience, and the relationship between architecture and territory into focus. Across the country, recent developments reflect different ways of understanding and responding to the conditions that shape the built environment, from the role of architecture in preserving collective memory to the challenges of adapting cities to environmental change. From cultural and public projects to heritage initiatives and new institutional developments, this month's selection explores how architecture responds to the evolving needs and identities of places and the communities that inhabit them.

The XIV Ibero-American Biennial in Brasília: Caring for Life Through Architecture and Urbanism.

The XIV Ibero-American Biennial of Architecture and Urbanism (BIAU) brought its 2026 edition to Brasília under the theme "Cuidar la Vida" (Caring for Life), placing the relationship between architecture, territory, and living conditions at the center of its program. Organized around four themes -water, vegetation, housing, and communities- the biennial brought together debates, exhibitions, lectures, and tours, while reflecting on Brasília's urban history and the tensions between modernist planning, territorial transformation, and contemporary living conditions. The edition recognized twelve works across its Projects and Publications categories, alongside five honorable mentions in the Projects category. The selected works addressed problems including access to housing, community life, environmental challenges, and the integration of natural systems into the built environment. Running from November 3 to 6, the program included exhibitions and discussions across venues such as SESI Lab, the University of Brasília, and the Teatro Nacional Cláudio Santoro.

Climate Resilience and Modern Architecture: Revisiting Brazil's Urban and Cultural Contexts.

The relationship between architecture, environmental conditions, and local identity also emerged through two stories examining different ways the built environment responds to its context. More than two years after the May 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul, the ongoing reconstruction of Porto Alegre and Cruzeiro do Sul raises questions about the long-term resilience of Brazilian cities and the extent to which rebuilding can address the planning decisions that contributed to their vulnerability. While Porto Alegre is strengthening its existing flood protection and drainage infrastructure, Cruzeiro do Sul is taking a different approach by relocating the severely affected Passo de Estrela neighborhood to higher ground. These contrasting strategies bring attention to the role of nature-based solutions, more adaptable urban planning, and the preservation of social networks in shaping recovery beyond the replacement of damaged buildings.

It has been revealed that questions of context and continuity also inform a retrospective on the work of architect Francisco de Assis Couto Reis (1926–2011), whose centenary was marked in October. Working primarily in Salvador, Bahia, Assis Reis developed an architectural language that connected modernist principles with local climatic, geographical, and cultural conditions, spanning projects from the headquarters of the São Francisco Hydroelectric Manufacturer (CHESF) to residential buildings and urban renewal proposals. The recent donation of his archive, comprising more than 3,000 items, to Casa da Arquitectura in Portugal further creates an opportunity to examine his design process and the broader contribution of his work to Brazilian modern architecture.

Brumadinho Memorial / Gustavo Penna Arquiteto e Associados.

Located at the site of the 2019 Córrego do Feijão dam collapse in Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, the Brumadinho Memorial by Gustavo Penna Arquiteto e Associados commemorates the 272 victims and provides a place for remembrance, reflection, and collective mourning. Developed in collaboration with the victims' families, the 1,220-square-meter project organizes its spaces along a 230-meter path excavated into the terrain, connecting the entrance pavilion to a lookout overlooking the transformed landscape. Concrete incorporating pigment from mining waste, carefully framed natural light, and a reflecting pool shape the visitor experience, while 272 yellow ipê trees honor each life lost. Opened to the public in 2025, the memorial brings architecture, landscape, and personal histories together to preserve memory and address the consequences of the tragedy.

Sertão Block and Amparo House / Asa Arquitetos.

Industry observers note that located in the rural area of Princesa Isabel, in the Paraíba hinterland, Sertão Block and Amparo House by Asa Arquitetos responds to the site's topography, climate, and landscape. Completed in 2026, the 622-square-meter residence is organized into independent volumes connected by verandas, courtyards, and terraces, drawing on the spatial principles of traditional rural estates. Large openings, hollow brick elements, and deep roof overhangs support natural ventilation and solar protection, while natural stone, wood, and ceramic bricks establish a material connection with the region. Built directly on a rocky outcrop, the separate Sertão Block functions as a private lookout over the surrounding landscape. The project reinterprets regional building practices through a contemporary approach to site, materiality, and climate.

Veras Cultural Center / Terra e Tuma Arquitetos Associados.

Located on the urban fringe of the Córrego Grande hills in Florianópolis, the Veras Cultural Center by Terra e Tuma Arquitetos Associados brings together cultural, educational, and environmental activities within a 1,100-square-meter building. Completed in 2023, the project is organized vertically to accommodate shared programs, including exhibition spaces, open studios, workshops, a restaurant, a market, and a rooftop community garden. Its concrete structure, exposed brick surfaces, and carefully positioned openings establish a relationship with the surrounding green areas while responding to the western sun. Conceived as a platform for community exchange, the center supports access to art and environmental education, bringing different forms of knowledge and cultural practices into a shared setting.

UNESCO Adds Three Brazilian Sites of Slavery Remembrance to Its International Memory Network.

Industry observers note that UNESCO has included three Brazilian sites in its Network of Historic and Memorial Sites Related to Slavery and the Slave Trade: Valongo Wharf in Rio de Janeiro, Sociedade Protetora dos Desvalidos in Salvador, and Serra da Barriga in União dos Palmares, Alagoas. The recognition highlights places that preserve different aspects of Afro-Brazilian history, from one of the Americas' principal landing points for enslaved Africans to a historic Black civil institution and the territory of Quilombo dos Palmares, an important center of resistance to slavery. Established in 2024, the network promotes the preservation and interpretation of sites associated with slavery through education, research, and international cooperation, connecting historic places with contemporary discussions on cultural heritage, collective memory, and the recognition of Black history.

Yuri Vital Arquiteto Wins Competition for UFC Arts and Culture Center in Fortaleza, Brazil.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Escritório Yuri Vital (@yurivitalarquiteto).

Sources indicate that são Paulo-based practice Yuri Vital Arquiteto has won the national architecture competition for the Arts, Culture and Events Center at the Federal University of Ceará (UFC) in Fortaleza, with a proposal selected from 64 submissions. Announced on November 5, 2026, the preliminary winning design will occupy the site of the former São Pedro Building, connecting the upcoming facility to the university's Iracema Campus. The approximately 11,000-square-meter, 14-story complex is planned to accommodate a cinema, exhibition spaces, a library, multipurpose rooms, and a performance hall. At ground level, the proposal introduces a public square with shaded pathways and spaces for gathering, while terraces, a rooftop garden, and an open-air amphitheater extend the cultural program into the urban landscape. Sources indicate that conventional construction often begins with a specification: a particular brick, concrete mix, manufactured panel or finish selected for a proposed building. What changes when the design process begins with a material that has already been recovered, produced or made available? Conventional construction often begins with a specification: a particular brick, concrete mix, manufactured panel or finish selected for a proposed building. What changes when the design process begins with a material that has already been recovered, produced or made available? Today, projects approach material resources through different processes: recovery, recycling and the engineering of locally sourced bamboo. Taken together, the varied approaches will show how material sourcing and processing can influence architectural decisions before a product reaches the building site.

Working with recovered or locally available materials introduces a different set of conditions into the design process. Recovered components rarely arrive in standardized dimensions or predictable quantities. Architects need to establish how many usable components are available, what condition they are in and whether their dimensions suit the proposed application. The available stock can influence the building's dimensions, the distribution of materials and the sequence of construction.

It has been revealed that the architects relate the screen to traditional Indonesian latticework, adapting the use of patterned openings and filtered light through a system of recycled-plastic plates and tensioned cables. In a 2020 systematic review published in Waste Management & Research, Kambiz Rakhshan and colleagues classify barriers to building-component reuse as economic, technical, social, regulatory and organisational. Concerns about component quality, regulatory compliance, liability and cost can make architects and contractors reluctant to specify recovered materials. Wider use will depend on reliable systems for assessing components, documenting their condition, establishing liability and coordinating procurement.

Recent findings suggest that life-cycle assessment can help compare the environmental impacts of material systems, provided the scope and assumptions of each assessment are clear. Eco-Mantra's life-cycle assessment of BaleBio reports a 110 percent reduction in Stage A emissions against its stated conventional baseline. The result is attributed primarily to the bamboo system, including the carbon stored in the material and the impacts associated with its production and transport. The result applies to BaleBio's stated assessment boundary and baseline; it cannot be generalized to other bamboo products, reclaimed materials or locally sourced components. Any wider comparison would also need to account for service life, maintenance, transport and end-of-life treatment.

  • In a recent development, the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) has selected Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA as the recipient of the first Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) has selected Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA as the recipient of the first Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture. The prize goes to the Dhaka-based architectural office for the design of the Friendship Centre, a rural training facility in Gaibandha, Bangladesh, inspired by one of the country's oldest urban archaeological sites. The prize, which MoMA describes as the largest award for a single architecture project, aims to recognize architectural practice while supporting tangible environmental action. Eligible projects may have been completed anywhere in the world in the past 30 years and must be considered exemplary in repairing architecture's relationship with nature. On this occasion, the $200,000 award is shared between the architect and the Fundación Gran Chaco, a nonprofit organization in Formosa, Argentina, which will plant trees in the Gran Chaco forest in the name of the project's client, the Friendship NGO, to contribute to reforestation efforts.

In a recent development, the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) has selected Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA as the recipient of the first Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture. The prize goes to the Dhaka-based architectural office for the design of the Friendship Centre, a rural training facility in Gaibandha, Bangladesh, inspired by one of the country's oldest urban archaeological sites. The prize, which MoMA describes as the largest award for a single architecture project, aims to recognize architectural practice while supporting tangible environmental action. Eligible projects may have been completed anywhere in the world in the past 30 years and must be considered exemplary in repairing architecture's relationship with nature. On this occasion, the $200,000 award is shared between the architect and the Fundación Gran Chaco, a nonprofit organization in Formosa, Argentina, which will plant trees in the Gran Chaco forest in the name of the project's client, the Friendship NGO, to contribute to reforestation efforts.

According to recent reports, the prize is named after Argentine-American architect and industrial designer Emilio Ambasz, who was curator of design at MoMA between 1968 and 1976. He has also served as a member of MoMA's International Council continuously since 1978 and was on the board of directors of MoMA PS1 from 2002 to 2006. In 2020, he donated funds to establish the Emilio Ambasz Institute for the Joint Study of the Built and the Natural Environment, which aims to give visibility to forms of interaction between architecture and ecology, facilitating dialogue and research. Its work seeks to strengthen the relevance of cultural and art institutions for today's diverse audiences through research and programs such as panels, conferences, lectures and conversations. According to Evangelos Kotsioris, director of the institute, the inaugural prize extends this approach by recognizing architecture that merges environmental adaptation, historical continuity, and sensitivity to the communities it serves.

Industry observers note that the prize is named after Argentine-American architect and industrial designer Emilio Ambasz, who was curator of design at MoMA between 1968 and 1976. He has also served as a member of MoMA's International Council continuously since 1978 and was on the board of directors of MoMA PS1 from 2002 to 2006. In 2020, he donated funds to establish the Emilio Ambasz Institute for the Joint Study of the Built and the Natural Environment, which aims to give visibility to forms of interaction between architecture and ecology, facilitating dialogue and research. Its work seeks to strengthen the relevance of cultural and art institutions for today's diverse audiences through research and programs such as panels, conferences, lectures and conversations. According to Evangelos Kotsioris, director of the institute, the inaugural prize extends this approach by recognizing architecture that merges environmental adaptation, historical continuity, and sensitivity to the communities it serves.

Describing the awarded project, Kotsioris says it "demonstrates how a remarkable economy of means can yield a richness of spatial experience, offering a compelling vision of how architecture might reconcile with nature." Completed in 2011, the Friendship Centre is a rural training facility and meeting space for communities in Bangladesh's flood-prone Jamuna River delta. The region is vulnerable to seasonal flooding and earthquakes, and the project responds with a compacted earthen embankment for flood protection and by building directly on the original, low-lying ground. The building was handcrafted mostly with local clay bricks, following community building traditions. The facility includes offices, classrooms, a library, meditation spaces, dormitories, and dining facilities distributed across two blocks. Its layout and image echo the nearby third-century BCE ancient city of Mahasthangarh, while adding contemporary elements such as green roofs, open-air courtyards and interconnected rainwater harvesting pools for temperature control and natural ventilation.

The Friendship Centre has been in service to an underserved community for 14 years. Yet, it is not a building of 14 years of age, but rather 2,300 years of age, as it draws its inspiration for flood protection from the nearby third-century BC settlement of Mahasthan. We are delighted that its coexistence with the surrounding agricultural, rural landscape, without really showing its mass forms to adjoining villages, has been recognized in this notable judgment. This pronouncement surely will, in no small terms, encourage an alternative reading of landscape and place making, not only in such locales as this remote part of one of the largest deltas in the world, but in every place where human intervention is destined to exist in the fragile ecosystem that we ourselves have caused to create. — Kashef Chowdhury.

In a recent development, kashef Chowdhury/URBANA's Friendship Centre was selected from a group of nearly 140 international projects, identified through research by the Ambasz Institute and proposals from 30 nominators representing different world regions. According to Martino Stierli, MoMA's Philip Johnson Chief Curator of Architecture and Design, the project was recognized as an example that leads architectural practices and design thinking into progressive new directions. The jury was composed of three representatives of MoMA's Department of Architecture and Design (Stierli; Evangelos Kotsioris, director of the Ambasz Institute and curator; and Paula Vilaplana de Miguel, assistant curator) and two external members: Shelley McNamara of Grafton Architects and Wang Shu of Amateur Architecture Studio. Projects were evaluated on rigor, creative engagement with the natural environment and alignment with the mission of the Emilio Ambasz Institute.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

London-based analytics firm GlobalData stated annual global solar PV additions will decline in 2026 for the first time since 2018, after rising 17.5% to a record in 2025. It attributed the slowdown to market reforms in China, policy changes in the United States and a slowdown in Pakistan.

“The 2026 dip reflects policy shifts in a few large markets rather than a weakening of solar’s fundamentals, with China’s move to market-based tariffs accounting for most of the decline,” said Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, a power analyst at GlobalData.

The organization mentioned it expects global cumulative PV capacity to grow at a compound annual rate of 12.5% from 2025 to 2035, more than doubling solar’s share of global electricity.

According to recent reports, china accounted for more than half of 2025 additions, followed by the United States and India. India’s additions rose 87.2%, and Pakistan’s grew 34.3% as rooftop and off-grid demand made it the fourth-largest market. Additions in the Middle East and Africa nearly tripled, while Europe’s rose 2.6% and North America’s fell 3.6%, remarked GlobalData.

Sources indicate that the organization noted the long decline in module prices has stalled, as higher silver and cell costs, China’s export tax rebate adjustment in April and Beijing’s “anti-involution” campaign pushed prices up in early 2026. Saibasan said grid constraints are now the main barrier to growth, pointing to curtailment in China, negative power prices in Europe and connection queues in the United States, India and Brazil.

Sources indicate that “Falling battery costs are the main counterweight to grid congestion, curtailment, and negative power prices. Solar-plus-storage is now competitive for firm supply in high-resource regions, allowing solar to move beyond daytime generation and compete for round-the-clock supply,” he said. “Developers and investors that pair solar with storage and secure grid access early will be best placed to capture the recovery from 2027.”.

The forecast follows GlobalData’s March projection that global solar capacity will reach 6 TW by 2031. The International Energy Agency’s Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme has estimated that global solar additions hit 690 GW in 2025, and in October the International Energy Agency forecast an 11% fall in global renewable capacity additions in 2026, mainly because of slower solar deployment in China.

  • Recent findings suggest that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

In a recent development, earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

Recent findings suggest that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially key, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

It has been revealed that experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Tech giant.
  • But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England.
  • Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Tech giant. An activist as well as an artist and businessman, he loathed the inequity of Victorian society and the soullessness of the industrial age, coming to embrace revolutionary socialism.

But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England. “Anything handmade is expensive,” she notes. “And it should be expensive, because of the labor that goes into it.”.

Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma. In a way, it seems, his goal of art for all may finally have been realized.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 concern of Smithsonian magazine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that they may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

One baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest revealed off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

In a recent development, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Nuclear submarine returns from record-breaking 217 days underwater

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater.
  • “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.
  • The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater. The HMS Vengeance’s seven-month deployment overtook the 205-day milestone set by the HMS Vanguard in April. But with the Vengeance crew finally back home, critics now argue the two submarines’ lengthy back-to-back voyages are causes for concern, not celebration.

“The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles. First introduced in 1998, the vessel features 16 missile tubes, each loaded with one Trident containing up to a dozen, 100-kiloton multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). The MIRV is specifically engineered to simultaneously deploy a payload of individual nuclear weapons aimed at a list of targets. The Royal Navy continuously keeps at least one Vanguard submarine at sea, which hypothetically allows the United Kingdom to still conduct nuclear strikes in the event its land-based systems are compromised during a nuclear war.

Vanguard submarines were originally built to host around 140 crewmembers during three-to-four month deployments. Although a 100-day excursion was once considered rare, underwater stints are now often double the length of time, forcing sailors to stack extra provisions along already cramped corridors and inside any additional nooks. The U.K. government attributes the extended missions to budgetary cuts that have dramatically slowed down the pace of multimillion-dollar vessel maintenance projects.

It has been revealed that deployment aboard a submarine like the Vengeance is considered one of the navy’s most psychologically difficult assignments. The nuclear sub remains underwater in total radio silence for the entire length of a patrol to keep its position secret. The vessel can travel to a depth of around 984 feet, but it may occasionally ascend to shallower waters to communicate via a transmission buoy or floating wire antenna. Crewmembers may receive a weekly, 120-word “Familygram” message, but each dispatch is previewed by naval officials. These readers retain the right to censor any bad news or information they feel may compromise sailors’ effectiveness. Regardless of what a sailor ultimately reads, they are strictly prohibited from responding.

The toll on crew is steep, but it’s particularly difficult for the women comprising roughly 10-percent of the navy. In 2022, whistleblower Sophie Brook generated international headlines after reporting a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” while serving as one of the Royal Navy’s first female submariners. In 2024, First Sea Lord Adm. Sir Ben Key called the crew misogyny “intolerable” and apologized to the growing number of women who subsequently came forward with their own stories. The Royal Navy’s investigations ultimately resulted in the firing, demotion, and disciplining of dozens of servicemen—including Key’s own termination.

Recent findings suggest that key’s successor, Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, stated he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for Trident crews earlier this month, while admitting the need to “improve our submarine maintenance.”.

Industry observers note that the Vanguard fleet was designed for about 25 years of service, but will likely accumulate roughly four decades of sailing by the time its first replacement is ready. That submarine, the HMS Dreadnought, isn’t expected to sail until around 2032.

#330. Latest Update: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (916 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Latest Update: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.
  • Industry observers note that ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
  • The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.

Industry observers note that ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The mission will examine the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) collision, helping scientists better understand how the technique could one day be used to protect Earth from incoming space rocks.

The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter. They form a binary asteroid system, a pair of asteroids that are gravitationally bound, orbiting each other around a shared center of mass.

Industry observers note that in September 2022, the golf-cart-size DART spacecraft intentionally struck the smaller celestial body in the world’s first demonstration of asteroid deflection technology. The mission not only successfully collided with Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around its major sibling by 33 minutes; it also altered the asteroid pair’s route around the sun. Now, Hera is returning to the crash scene to follow up on that work.

“Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene,” Patrick Michel, a planetary scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research and Hera’s principal investigator, tells Meghan Bartels for Space.com.

The spacecraft, which is about the size of a small car, performed its first arrival maneuver on October 15, and ESA released Hera’s first close-up photo of the asteroid duo on November 5. The picture, snapped about 37 miles from the rocky pair, prominently features Didymos, with the smaller Dimorphos mostly hidden in the larger asteroid’s shadow.

In a recent development, while looking at this image, “the first thing we noted was wow!” Michel says in a statement. “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole latest world.”.

Recent findings suggest that on November 12, ESA released another image of the asteroid system, this time taken from about 35 miles away. It highlights one side of Didymos and a sliver of Dimorphos peeking out from behind the larger rock, on the upper left. This photo reveals various features on the bigger asteroid’s surface, including large boulders, smooth areas and a sharp ridge at the equator.

Scientists want to understand which of these and other characteristics were present long ago and which might be consequences of the DART impact.

According to recent reports, “Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately one kilometer of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out,” states Michael Küppers, a planetary scientist and Hera mission scientist at ESA, in the earlier statement. “We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.”.

It has been revealed that hera should now be within about 20 miles of the asteroid duo, per Space.com, and then move even closer in December. Then, early next year, the spacecraft will deploy two shoebox-size CubeSats. These nanosatellites, equipped with radar and spectral instruments, will fly in and examine the surfaces and inner structures of the asteroids. One of the devices, called Juventas, will attempt to land on Dimorphos to capture more information about the asteroid’s surface material and gravity field.

According to recent reports, did you know? Complementary design.

The DART and Hera missions were intentionally designed to go together, with the first performing the deflection and the second collecting precise measurements of the outcome.

These studies will not just help experts develop techniques for planetary defense in case an object one day poses a danger to Earth; they’ll also advance our understanding of asteroids in general.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” notes Jessica Sunshine, a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission, to Bartels for Science News. On the science side, she adds, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

Industry observers note that one question she and other researchers hope Hera will help answer relates to the system’s stabilization post-impact. Previously, Dimorphos always indicated the same face to Didymos as it circled its companion, like the moon does with Earth. Researchers suspect DART changed that, and they want to see how it’ll reset, per Science News. Additionally, they want to better understand how exposure to charged particles affects an asteroid’s surface. The debris kicked up on Dimorphos by DART can help them examine fresh rock that was previously protected from those particles.

Detailed images of both asteroids will be unveiled on November 25, according to the earlier statement.

Recent findings suggest that “For us, it’s like a new world,” Michel tells Space.com. “The new image won’t have anything to do with the previous one, so that’s really exciting.”.

#326. More Than a Billion Years' Worth of Rock Layers Are Missing From Earth's Geologic Record. Scientists Say They May Finally Know Why

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (701 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

More Than a Billion Years' Worth of Rock Layers Are Missing From Earth's Geologic Record. Scientists Say They May Finally Know Why

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top.
  • Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.
  • In a recent development, computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top. But a giant, mysterious gap exists in many of the globe’s landmasses. It’s well-documented in North America, northern Europe and northern China, where in some places more than one billion years of our planet’s geologic record is nowhere to be found.

Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.

In a recent development, computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Nature, help validate some of the possible explanations about the Great Unconformity, possibly solving the 150-year-old mystery.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story,” says study co-author Santosh Dhungana, an Earth scientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, in a statement. “Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance.”.

Did you know? The Grand Canyon’s role.

Researchers first described the Great Unconformity in the late 1800s in the layers of the Grand Canyon.

It has been revealed that many scientists suspect that during the planet’s theorized Snowball Earth period, when the entire planet may have been frozen some 635 million to 720 million years ago, moving ice scraped away the missing rock layers. But if ice sheets covered the globe, they should have eroded the Great Unconformity everywhere, which isn’t the case, reports Ars Technica’s Jacek Krywko.

Sources indicate that some researchers have also hypothesized that mantle movements, which alter the planet’s surface, could be to blame. In the viscous mantle, hotter material rises and cooler material falls, pushing and pulling Earth’s outer layer, called the crust. However, this concept of mantle-driven dynamic topography “hadn’t been quantitatively tested,” study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, tells Ars Technica.

It has been revealed that so, he and Dhungana used computer models to simulate these mantle movements, called convection, over the past billion years. Their six models “consistently showed that mantle convection caused ancient continental blocks Laurentia (which now makes up much of North America), Baltica (parts of northern Europe) and North China to be lifted up from around a billion years ago to 540 million years ago,” the authors write for the Conversation. Over the past 540 million years, however, these continental chunks have sunk.

Industry observers note that the era of continental uplift overlaps with the Snowball Earth period, and giant moving ice sheets erode landscapes more efficiently than rivers. The scientists speculate that the frozen masses would have ground their way down the slopes of raised landscapes, wiping away millions of years’ worth of rock accumulation.

What’s more, the Great Unconformity intrigues scientists interested in life’s history because it wiped the rock record just before the Cambrian explosion around 530 million years ago, when all sorts of animals suddenly evolved.

In a recent development, the geologic processes that took place during the Great Unconformity may have created the foundation for this famous evolutionary event, Shanan Peters, a geoscientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who did not participate in the study, tells Live Science’s Stephanie Pappas. By exposing older crystalline rocks, for example, the erosion may have triggered a greater release of certain elements, such as potassium, iron, manganese and carbon, into the oceans, allowing marine life to invent shells. That, in turn, may have put more oxygen into Earth’s atmosphere, Peters adds.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see,” Flament claims in the statement.

#325. Solar recycling 2.0

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1715 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Solar recycling 2.0

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A number of companies in the United States are vying to leverage capital, experience, and upcoming technology ahead of a wave of end-of-life solar panels expected in the coming years.
  • According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the annual volume of end-of-life crystalline silicon modules in the US is expected to hit 87,000 metric tons (MT) by 2030 and skyrocket to 820,000 MT by 2050.
  • With that volume comes economic opportunity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A number of companies in the United States are vying to leverage capital, experience, and upcoming technology ahead of a wave of end-of-life solar panels expected in the coming years.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the annual volume of end-of-life crystalline silicon modules in the US is expected to hit 87,000 metric tons (MT) by 2030 and skyrocket to 820,000 MT by 2050.

With that volume comes economic opportunity. In 2023, analysts at Rystad Energy estimated the global value of recycled solar materials would hit $2.7 billion in 2030, rising to $80 billion by 2050. Assuming a 15-year panel lifespan, Rystad’s research estimated end-of-life solar modules in North America would be worth $1.4 billion in 2037 – about 15% of the global total.

This article appears in a special edition of pv magazine, produced for RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas. Scan or Click for free access to the full 54-page magazine, packed with the latest from the US solar and energy storage industries.

Sources indicate that most of the material in a solar module is glass, which typically accounts for between 70% and 76% of a module’s weight. The second-largest portion is the aluminum frame, accounting for between 8% and 13%. But the most valuable material inside most solar modules is silver.

Industry observers note that silver now represents an key strategic asset to the United States. Along with silicon, ­silver was added to the US Critical Minerals List in November 2025.

In solar manufacturing, paste formed with the precious metal is screen printed in thin lines onto the surface of a silicon solar cell to collect and transport electrical current. It accounts for around 60% of the cost of those cells, and 10% of the total cost of a solar module.

According to the IEA, solar silver consumption was around 10 mg/W in 2024, down from 16 mg/W in 2020. While this equates to only about 0.05% of a panel’s total weight, the concentration of silver in a solar module rivals that found in many silver ores currently being mined.

That number was even higher for modules produced further in the past, meaning the coming wave of end-of-life modules will be rich in their most valuable component. The trouble is, once the cells are sealed inside layers of encapsulant, the metal contents have proven very difficult to recover without a high-temperature smelting process.

It is common practice for PV recycling companies to separate the glass and frame on the outside of a module, while the laminated components on the inside are shredded and sent to other recyclers often overseas, or even to landfill.

“The industry as a whole up to now has been on a 1.0 system, if you will,” said Adam Saghei, CEO of We Recycle Solar (WRS), in an interview with pv magazine USA. “It’s about shredding. It is heavily dependent on a mechanical process.”.

When that shredded material is exported, the valuable silver, silicon, copper, and other trace metals trapped in the encapsulant are exported, too.

According to recent reports, in addition, the recovered glass often contains impurities that make it unsuitable for use in high-temperature, closed-loop remanufacturing, such as new solar glass, instead of being used in “down-cycled” applications such as road base, concrete aggregate, and sandblasting media. All of that is changing now.

A number of US companies have developed alternative technologies to capture a much greater proportion of valuable solar materials and sell them domestically.

In September, WRS declared that it planned to open what it called “the nation’s first end-to-end critical materials recovery facility for retired solar panels” on a 10-acre site in Dallas, Texas, by the third quarter of 2027. The company says its “recycling 2.0” process allows it to recover up to 96% of the silver, copper, silicon, aluminum, and glass from end-of-life solar panels.

Sources indicate that “Our approach is a little bit different,” said Saghei. “It’s on a very small footprint with regenerative solvents.” He added that the process results in glass with less than 10 parts per million of impurities. “That is essentially pure enough for you to drink out of. It’s as pure as glass comes.”.

In a recent development, meanwhile, OnePlanet Solar has been operating its commercial demonstration plant in Florida since early 2024. The plant is capable of processing 480,000 end-of-life solar modules in a year, equal to around 19,000 tons of material. According to the organization, 100% of the outputs of this facility have been sold and consumed within the United States.

In a recent development, in August 2026, OnePlanet unveiled its upcoming “PRISM” process (short for “Photovoltaic Recycling through Integrated Systems and Mechanics”). The firm notes PRISM results in 99% pure glass before any size reduction step, for both single side and bifacial modules, and also yields a concentrated silicon product with 95% purity that contains 1% silver.

Recycling of end-of-life modules using the PRISM process is expected to begin in 2027, and OnePlanet’s next goal is to refine its own metallurgical-grade silicon (MGS) while capturing the silver as a secondary finished product.

Industry observers note that another US firm building out its recycling capabilities is Comstock Metals, which is now in the beginning stages of operating a solar recycling facility in Silver Springs, Nevada. The facility was first commissioned and tested in August 2026, and the company is working to ramp the plant up to 25% of its rated output capacity of 100,000 tons per year.

Comstock is also practicing a upcoming, proprietary process at the Silver Spring site, designed to completely decompose adhesives, encapsulant, and plastic materials before the remaining components of the panel are sorted and separated for additional processing. Judd Merrill, the organization’s chief financial officer, explained that the company’s current strategy is to retain the metal-rich material for its own proprietary metals recovery process.

Comstock’s aims for that metal recovery process start with a pilot-scale metals recovery operation, also planned for Silver Springs. “We are developing proprietary extraction and recovery technologies specifically designed to process the concentrated material generated by our solar recycling system. That material contains multiple valuable metals and other recoverable materials, and our objective is to recover those materials into marketable products for domestic reuse without conventional smelting,” mentioned Merrill.

Comstock’s goal is to have a pilot-scale metal recovery line “operating continuously and reliably” by the end of 2026.

A key step in the success of any business is the development of ongoing relationships with partners. For solar recyclers, those relationships are made with entities on both sides of the recycling process.

On the supply side, this means contracting with manufacturers, EPCs, and re-powering companies. Comstock, for example, has minted deals with RWE for decommissioning aged solar panels as well as agreeing to take manufacturing byproducts from solar manufacturer Illuminate USA.

Sources indicate that similarly, leading recycler Solarcycle has partnered with Silfab, Canadian Solar, and Qcells to recycle factory defects and has inked agreements with major developers including Sunrun, EDP Renewables, AES, Orsted, and Greenbacker. The firm has also confirmed public offtake agreements for the outputs of its recycling process. It has signed agreements with Silfab and Illuminate USA for new solar glass made from recycled modules.

Solarcycle is at the moment in the process of building a 1.1 million square foot glass plant next to its existing recycling facility in Cedartown, Georgia. With glass production at the facility slated to begin in 2028, the company is targeting enough glass production to support up to 6 GW of domestic panel assembly annually.

As of 2025, the NC Clean Energy Technology Center tracked 23 states with mandatory statewide decommissioning policies. Despite the widespread nature of those policies, laws in just four states (California, Maine, New Jersey, and New York) effectively prohibit the disposal of solar panels in landfills and dumps.

Outside those states, and in the absence of federal regulation, entities seeking to responsibly offload those products usually engage recyclers based on their own corporate ESG goals.

It has been revealed that obtaining quality and traceability certifications has become a key way recyclers set themselves apart from their competitors. Recyclers often pursue certification under ISO standards 9001 (Quality Management Systems), 14001 (Environmental Management Systems), and 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety).

In addition to obtaining those certifications, many companies seek listing under the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) National PV Recycling Program, which requires a facility audit and analysis of a tech giant’s operations. SEIA at the moment lists 16 companies as partners under the program.

According to recent reports, recyclers seeking to go one step further obtain a certification from Sustainable Electronics Recycling International (SERI), which certifies PV recyclers under Appendix G of the third version of its Responsible Recycling (R2v3) standard. R2v3 requires annual surveillance audits by accredited certification bodies and complete chain of custody documentation for all materials. It also enforces safe handling procedures for panels, solar glass processing standards, and silicon wafer recovery protocols.

At the time of writing, SERI lists 30 facilities with active R2v3 certifications in North America, including the Comstock and OnePlanet facilities.

“Our view of certifications is pretty straightforward,” Connor Hogan, CFO of OnePlanet, told pv magazine USA. “If you can get a certification, you should just get a certification rather than say that you can attest to it.”.

Industry observers note that other companies aren’t as keen on R2v3. “One glitch with R2 certification is that it’s kind of open source, and when you spend years cultivating a relationship with a downstream partner, you don’t want to just give that up so everyone knows who you’re selling material to,” remarked Saghei, adding that “certifications are like a driver’s license – just because everyone has one doesn’t mean they’re a good driver.”.

In the coming years, solar recyclers will find many ways to differentiate themselves based on the effectiveness and economics of their logistics and recovery processes, as well as the adaptability of those processes and how swiftly they can scale operations.

It has been revealed that the relationships recyclers build with manufacturers, developers, downstream offtakers, and policymakers will also be essential. They will face questions from those stakeholders about their certifications and material tracing practices and will likely be presented with fresh challenges as state governments take action to ensure solar module waste is recycled properly.

#324. Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet.
  • Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances.
  • Industry observers note that “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, remarked in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

Industry observers note that “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, remarked in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”.

Recent findings suggest that bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

The earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into fresh species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

According to recent reports, their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now shows that it’s a snipe.

Recent findings suggest that “Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as newly introduced species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”.

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

According to recent reports, “These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” remarked Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”.
